body.p: In view of the claim amendments and below remarks, the Examiner is respectfully requested to reconsider the rejections. The Applicant thanks the Examiner for the determination of allowable subject matter.
Advisory Action Summary

The Examiner disagreed with the arguments filed by Applicant August 21, 2024. Further, the amendments filed August 21, 2024 were not entered, the Advisory Action indicating regarding the amendments that "They raise new issues that would require further consideration and/or search" and "They are not deemed to place the application in better form for appeal by materially reducing or simplifying the issues for appeal." As the amendments were not entered, the claims currently remain rejected for the same reasons as in the final rejection mailed June 20, 2024.

Claim 17 was previously amended within the August 21, 2024 response to remove the term 'readily', and to recite that the health or fitness tracker application does not process the radio frequency based data. Claim 31 was amended similarly. Support for these amendment is within the filed specification at page 4, lines 11-14 that describes (bolding added): "However, this RF based data may not be readily processed by health and fitness tracker applications having application programming interfaces (APIs) accustomed to operating with, for example, sensor data, such as x-y-z accelerometer data or other types of sensor data, indicative of the user's activity."
It is therefore respectfully submitted that claims 17 and 31 are now definite, and the Examiner is respectfully requested to withdraw the rejections based on Section 112.

The Examiner is respectfully requested to withdraw the rejections based on Section 103, because the prior art does not disclose or suggest the subject matter of the independent claims. MPEP 2143.03 (all claim limitations must be considered).

body.p: Support for this amendment is within the filed specification at page 8, lines 8-17 and page 10, lines 2-9.

Gillilan paragraph [0093] describes "At 608, a radar feature indicative of a characteristic of the target is extracted from the radar data. The radar feature may provide a real-time measurement of the characteristic of the target, position of the target, or dynamics of the target. The radar feature may include any suitable type of feature, such as a detection feature, reflection feature, motion feature, position feature, or shape feature, examples of which are described herein. In the context of the present example, reflection radar features and motion radar features of the user's hand are extracted from the radar data."

Stivoric paragraph [0223] describes "Under such conditions, for example, if a sensor, for example an accelerometer, fails, the system might conclude that the wearer is sleeping or resting or that no motion is taking place. Under such conditions it is very hard to conclude if the data is bad or if the model that is predicting and making the conclusion is wrong. When an application involves both model and data uncertainties, it is very important to identify the relative magnitudes of the uncertainties associated with data and the model. An intelligent system would notice that the sensor seems to be producing erroneous data and would either switch to alternate algorithms or would, in some cases, be able to fill the gaps intelligently before making any predictions."

The Examiner stated on page 4 of the Office Action, regarding claim 16, that Gillian at the above-referenced excerpt ([0093]) describes the claimed aspect related to the pseudo sensor data being provided during a time interval. The Examiner applies the same rationale to reject the
corresponding aspects of claim 27 (Office Action, page 18) and claim 35 (Office Action, page 28).

The Examiner stated on pages 5-6 of the Office Action that Stivoric at the above-referenced excerpt ([0223]) describes a time interval when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user is not provided or is unavailable. The Examiner also stated that Stivoric at the above- referenced excerpt ([0223]) describes a time interval when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user is not provided or is unavailable, to reject claim 27 (Office Action, page 19) and claim 35 (Office Action, page 29).
The Examiner also stated within the Advisory Action that Gillian teaches providing the pseudo sensor data during a time interval, and Stivoric teaches that time interval (underlining added):

Gillian at paragraph [0093] at best describes providing a radar feature. Stivoric at paragraph [0223] at best describes switching to an alternate algorithm in response to a failure or data being provided erroneously. Neither Gillian nor Stivoric describe a time from when the native sensor data is not provided to a time when the pseudo sensor data begins to be provided being less than a threshold amount of time.
The Examiner also stated that the motivation to combine Stivoric with Gillian would be provide a continuous stream of data in the case of device failure to prevent bad data or wrong
conclusions from being made:

In contrast, in Applicant's case, Applicant within the filed specification describes such an implementation detail, including at page 8, lines 11-17 which describes "However, if there is a time during which the sensor 399 cannot generate sensor data (e.g., due to charging or for other reasons as noted), this time may be considered a gap in the continuous stream of sensor data. In some embodiments, the gap may be defined by a predefined time where there is no sensor data, such as 2 minutes (although other times may be used as well), while in some embodiments, the gap may be defined by a message or trigger signal indicating that the sensor 399 is not able to generate sensor data."

Thus in Applicant's case, the gap in time from when the native sensor data stops being provided to when the pseudo sensor data is provided is considered a threshold amount of time, such that the gap is no more than the threshold amount of time. For example, as indicated within Applicant's specification (at page 11, line 38 to page 12, line 2), a message or a trigger signal may be sent (e.g. by the health and fitness tracker 104 to the radio frequency based tracker 110) to indicate that the sensor of the health and fitness tracker 104 is not able generate sensor data, such that a time from when the native sensor data is not provided to a time when the pseudo sensor data begins to be provided is less than a threshold amount of time.

This is also discussed within Applicant's filed specification at page 10, lines 6-9, which describes (bolding added) "In this way, the pseudo sensor data can fill in at least a portion of a gap (as shown at FIG. 3B at 370, for example) to enable providing a more continuous, or nearly continuous, stream of data for health and fitness tracking by the application 390, the health and fitness tracker 104, and/or the like."
The embodiment now claimed in the independent claims (claims 16, 27, 35) may be illustrated as follows:

Such embodiments related to a time from when the native sensor data is not provided to a time when the pseudo sensor data begins to be provided being less than a threshold amount of time are not disclosed or suggested by the combination of Stivoric and Gillian.

For these same reasons, new claim 36 is patentable, which recites "sending, by the second apparatus comprising the health and fitness tracker application to the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker, a trigger message that indicates to the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker to begin providing the pseudo sensor data; wherein the trigger

message that indicates to the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker to begin providing the pseudo sensor data that is sent by the second apparatus comprising the health and fitness tracker application is based on the threshold amount of time." Support for new claim 36 is within the filed specification at page 8, lines 8-17 and page 11, line 33 to page 12, line 4. The filed specification describes that the health and fitness tracker may send a trigger message to the radio frequency based tracker to initiate the providing of the pseudo sensor data, at page 11, line 38 to page 12, line 2 which describes "the health and fitness tracker 104 may trigger the RF based tracker 110 to track the user in response to the health and fitness tracker 104 transmitting an indication, such as by transmitting a trigger signal or sending a message, to the RF based tracker 110."

Accordingly, the prior art does not disclose or suggest wherein an amount of time between when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user that is associated with the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application begins to not be provided to the second apparatus or when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user begins to be unavailable to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application, and when the pseudo sensor data begins to be provided to the second apparatus using the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker, is less than a threshold amount of time. Independent claims 16, 27, and 35, on the other hand, claim "wherein an amount of time between when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user that is associated with the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application begins to not be provided to the second apparatus or when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user begins to be unavailable to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application, and when the pseudo sensor data begins to be provided to the second apparatus using the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker, is less than a threshold amount of time." This is not disclosed or suggested in the prior art. Therefore, independent claims 16, 27, and 35 are patentable and should be allowed.
2. Even if it was obvious to combine the references, they do not disclose or suggest all of the elements/features of the claims, as explained above
Applicant respectfully traverses the rationale to combine the references to support a rejection under Section 103. For example, even if, for the sake of argument, it was obvious to

combine the references, they do not disclose or suggest all of the elements/features of the claims as a whole, as explained above. When applying Section 103 to Applicant's claimed invention, the claimed invention should be considered as a whole per Hodosh v. Block Drug Co., Inc., 786 F.2d 1136, 1143 n.5 (Fed. Cir. 1986) ("when applying § 103: (1) the claimed invention must be considered as a whole").
3. Dependent claims

Though the dependent claims contain their own allowable subject matter, including new claims 36-37, these claims should at least be allowable due to their dependence from allowable independent claims. Support for new claims 36-37 is within the filed specification at page 8, lines 11-17. However, to expedite prosecution at this time, no further comment will be made.

The Applicant respectfully requests the Examiner enter this amendment and pass the claims to issue. The undersigned representative welcomes the opportunity to resolve any matters that may remain, formal or otherwise, via teleconference at the Examiner's discretion.
